lines: Drying weather, if it holds. I'll get the field done and the hens in, and then it can do what it likes.
Every night's the same here. Hens in at seven, and the hatch dropped. Sheep penned. Pump primed for the morning, so I'm not stood out at it at six.
Door bolted before the bell goes, up north. That's nine. Then I sit down. That's the whole of it, every night.
The barn? I chain it, after the hens. Did I not say? I chain it.
There's a card on the doors. I wrote it out myself, and I put please on it, and thank you. I don't know who I put them on for.
Keep to the road once the lamps are lit, mind. Things come up out of the rough ground after dark and stand along the verge. They don't come on, mostly.
I've watched them from the bedroom. They stand about like men waiting to be paid.
The crows have given up the plough. They follow folk along the fence now, post to post, and turn back at the last one.
I walked it twice to see. Both times it was the last post.
Oh, sorry, I didn't see you there. You're not from round here, are you. Sorry, I don't mean anything by it. Nobody walks the road now unless they have to.
I'm sorry, we lock the door at nine. You'd be welcome before, only once it's locked I don't go near it till morning. Everybody along here's the same. Sorry.
Sorry, I've the tea to get. The children aren't let out on the road after it. My mother was the same with me.
I never thought to ask her why. I'm sorry about that now, and there's nobody to ask.
Sorry, is it me, or are the lamps on earlier? I start the potatoes by them, and it's been sooner every week since March.
I'm sorry. You've not come all this way to hear about my potatoes.
Making for Castle? Keep to the road and you'll be there before the lamps. Don't cut across. The fields are bigger than they look. Wider, I mean. They go on.
You'll hear the School's bell at nine. It's rung every night I can remember. Every night since I was a boy, I should say.
Nobody's taught a lesson up there since I was a boy, either. Since before. My father never heard one.
They light the lamps at dusk and count them at ten. Counted, I mean. I counted them, for years, and it never came to the same number twice.
I'm careful. I was careful. I still am, I'd say.
I've stood about here most days for forty years. Forty-one. The road used to go somewhere else. Not far off. A field's width, it would be.

country_woman.speaker: A Woman in a Brown Coat

lines: You've come off the road, haven't you? I can see you have. Is it far to Castle from here? It isn't. I've walked it often enough. I don't know why I asked.
Do children argue when they're told to stay in? They do. Mine did, every night. I don't let them past the garden after tea.
They've stopped arguing. Is that a good thing? I don't think it is.
Has a man come by with a cart? He hasn't, has he. My husband went to see a man about one this morning. He said dinner time. I've kept his dinner hot twice.
Will you be walking on after dark? You will. Stay where the lamps are. Do you know what stands off the road at night? No. Nor do I. I've never gone to look.
You've come up off the road; you've the dust on you to the knee. Watch the stumps. I've not had them out yet.
I cut this side of the wood. Nobody cuts the other side, and it doesn't grow.
You'll be wanting home before the bell, same as me. You walk like somebody who does. It carries in a wood. You'd swear it was the next clearing over.
There's something in the trees after dark, bigger than a fox. Not you; you're too light on your feet. I've never seen it.
I've seen where it's lain down, though. It lies down facing the road.
You'd be the sort to mark a place, I'd say. I was. I leave the axe in a stump overnight, and in the morning it's never quite where I left it.
I used to cut a nick in the bark to be sure. I've stopped doing that.
Keep to the planks and the road. Planks and road. I lost a boot off the end of this landing in May, and I've cut here twenty years.
May. I've been over it since, and it was May.
The water's higher than it was. It's up two planks on the landing since the spring. I look every morning, and again at dinner, and again before I go in.
It doesn't rain any more than it used to.
I cut and stack by the hut. I count the bundles in at night, and count them again, and in the morning I count them out. A bundle or two short, most mornings.
Nothing I know of eats reed. I've counted again, in case.
If you hear somebody calling from out on the water, that'll be the herons. I've stood and listened, more than once. It's the herons. Mostly.
Rooms by the week, teas all day. Nobody's taken a room since the spring, but I keep them aired.
The commercial gentleman in the front likes his window an inch open, so I see to that. He takes his tea at four. He's very particular.
The lamp by the door's lit at dusk and I don't put it out. People on the road like to see a light. The commercial gentleman says it's the first thing he looks for.
Things off the road don't care for it, as far as I can tell.
Doors shut at nine. If anyone knocks after that, it isn't us they want. My husband goes down and listens at it, and comes back up, and says nothing.
I don't open to find out.
People point at the sign and ask halfway to where. My father painted it. He says it was halfway when he painted it, and I've never had a better answer off him.

country_man.speaker: A Man in a Grey Coat

lines: You'll be out after the lamps, I expect. You'll keep to where it's lit. I won't give you a reason. I'll be doing it myself, and I'll be here tomorrow.
You'll have come in on the Sunday train. It'll run every day again, they'll tell you, come the summer. They'll be saying it the summer after.
You'll hear the bell at nine tonight. It'll be louder than usual. Everybody I ask will tell me it wasn't, and I'll let them.
I'll be waiting for the carrier. He'll come on Tuesday.
It isn't Tuesday. I know it isn't. I'll be early, that's all. I like to be.
A woman comes to the door drying her hands on her apron. She's nothing to sell and nothing to buy, thank you.
She hopes I get where I'm going before the lamps. She says it twice, and shuts the door on the second time.
"Who is it?" A man's voice, close to the wood. Then: "No, thank you. We keep early hours out here." I hadn't asked him for anything.
Locked. Through the window: a table laid for four, the cups turned up ready, and three chairs.
I count the chairs again. Then I go, because it isn't my table.
A voice through the door says, not unkindly, that they don't open to people off the road. "Is it still light out? Then you've time to get on."
The voice doesn't come any nearer the door while it says it.
The light inside goes out while I'm still knocking. Nobody moves about in there. I'd hear them on the boards.
The door gives an inch and stops. Something heavy's been pushed against it from the inside. A dresser, by the sound.
Whoever pushed it there is on the inside too.
The doors are chained on the outside. A card pinned to them, lettered carefully: PLEASE DON'T LOOK IN THE BARN. THANK YOU.
I don't. The chain's on my side of the doors. I notice that.
Padlocked. The padlock's new and the shed isn't. I give it a tug anyway.
THE HALFWAY HOUSE. ROOMS. TEAS. Halfway to where, the sign doesn't say.
There's a bench in the porch, out of the wind. If it goes badly for me out there, this is where I'll wake.
THE HALFWAY HOUSE. ROOMS. A light behind the curtains upstairs.
The door opens before I've knocked twice. A woman in a dressing gown stands back to let me in. She doesn't ask my name, and she doesn't look past me at the road.

options.label: Sit in the porch a while

lines: The room's at the top of the stairs. I hear nothing all night.
In the morning nobody's about. The porch door's on the latch, and there's tea for me on the step.
I sit with my back to the door and my knees up. The night doesn't get any shorter for it. If it goes badly out there, this is where I'll wake.
A bucket on a chain. I drop a pebble and count. The water at the bottom is further down than the chain is long.
A candle in a box on a post. It was lit today; the wax round it is still soft. Nobody has passed me on this road.
EGGS. HONESTY BOX. I lift the lid. It's full of buttons, all sorts, a coat's worth.
Blankets, a tin plate wiped clean, and a pair of good boots, laced, with nobody's feet in them.
The earth at the mouth is worn smooth. Whatever uses it goes in and out every day, and it's a good deal bigger than a rabbit. I keep my hands in my pockets.
The hive's quiet. You're meant to tell the bees when somebody dies. Nobody's told these anything for a while.
I put my hand flat on the lid. I nearly tell them something.
An iron pump, the green paint worn off the handle where it's held. The water comes up cold on the second stroke. I drink out of my hand.
The name's worn away. The flowers on it are fresh; the stems are still wet where they were cut.
The hen goes round the same few spots, always in the same order, and stands at each one a while before she moves on. I watch her do it twice.
They keep to the same few yards of grass all day, though nothing's stopping them. Nobody brings them in. By the bell they're not here.
It doesn't run from me. As far as I can see, it doesn't run from anything.
